lessons.title: Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
lessons.concept: SDLC is a structured process for planning, creating, testing, and maintaining software. Common phases include requirements analysis, design, implementation (coding), testing, deployment, and maintenance. Different models (waterfall, iterative, agile) arrange these activities differently.
lessons.formula: Typical flow: Requirements -> Design -> Implementation -> Testing -> Deployment -> Maintenance.
lessons.worked_example: For a student portal app: gather requirements (login, grades view), design database/UI, implement features, test for bugs/security, deploy to users, and maintain with updates/fixes.
mistakes: Thinking SDLC ends at deployment (maintenance is ongoing)
Skipping requirements/design and jumping directly to coding
Assuming one SDLC model fits every project

lessons.title: Requirements and Design Basics
lessons.concept: Requirements define what the system should do (functional) and how well it should do it (non-functional, e.g., performance, security, usability). Design translates requirements into an architecture and component plan, including data models, interfaces, and modules.
lessons.formula: Functional: features/behaviors. Non-functional: quality attributes (performance, reliability, security, etc.).
lessons.worked_example: Functional: 'User can reset password via email.' Non-functional: 'Password reset email should be sent within 1 minute.' Design would specify components/services handling the reset flow.
mistakes: Confusing functional requirements with non-functional requirements

lessons.title: Testing and Maintenance
lessons.concept: Software testing verifies that the system meets requirements and finds defects. Levels include unit, integration, system, and acceptance testing. Maintenance involves correcting defects, adapting to changes, improving performance, and preventing future issues after release.
lessons.formula: Unit -> Integration -> System -> Acceptance (common progression). Maintenance types: corrective, adaptive, perfective, preventive.
lessons.worked_example: A unit test checks a single function (e.g., password validation). Integration testing checks that login module works with the database. After release, fixing a reported bug is corrective maintenance.
mistakes: Relying only on system testing and skipping unit/integration tests
Assuming testing guarantees bug-free software (it reduces risk)
Ignoring maintenance effort in project planning

options.B: Sequential phases where each must complete before the next begins
options.D: Being usable only for hardware projects
